title: DoD Sustainment Series Global Economic Conditions Contested Logistics Environment 1 Panel 2.15.22

cues.text: >> I'd like to thank everyone for joining today's DAU Event
of another episode of the DoD Sustainment Series.
Today is the Global Economic Conditions Keynote,
Moving Technology into Sustainment Panel, and Contested Logistics Panel.
My name is Emmett Simmons, I'm he producer for today's event.
Agenda for today's posted, your microphones will be muted, the session is being recorded,
and will be posted to dau.edu/events, and on the event page listed for today.
If you have any questions, please submit your questions via the chat.
If you're here for CLPs, the session does quality for up
to three CLPs with supervisor approval.
It is not automatic so you both need to apply for it.
There is a survey at the end and at the end of the survey there is a link that you can copy
and paste to get your CLP certificate.
Without further ado, I'm going to turn it over to Dr. Vic Ramdass
to introduce our speakers and get us kicked off.
>> Thanks, Emmet.
I'm Dr. Vic Ramdass.
I'm the DASD Material Readiness and I want to extend a special thank you for all
of those joining us from the out stations.
We've sort of gotten used to this COVID environment and conducting these panels.
The sustainment series emanated from the fact that we had
to postpone the maintenance symposium on a couple occasions.
So, this is our opportunity to really share with you some of the department's initiatives
on maintenance and also hear from you on those initiatives.
So, we have embarked on a data journey.
We now have routinely or reporting on business health metrics.
For the first time we have sustainment and acquisition metrics side-by-side.
We're in the process of staffing an issuance that will standardized how we report
on readiness in terms of operational availability,
material availability, MC, and ONS costs.
So, for the first time we're going to have all of that in a dashboard
and Advanta hosted here at the department level.
Before we get into our keynote speaker, just a couple of key dates that I want to share
with you that's important because I know some of you might part spin
in the first panel may not be here for a second.
But those dates are the next Sustainment Series of Element will be June of this year.
We also have the Air Force Software Enterprise
in Ogden Air Logistics Complex hosting the DoD Air and Space Weapons Systems Software Summit
in Salt Lake City and that's May 3-4 of this year.
We're hosting on May 19-20, or OIB Commanders Peer-to-Peer meeting.
And this is the first time we're going to have all of our commanders sit together
and really share lessons learned across the services.
And then, we hope to actually have a 2022 DoD Maintenance Symposium, which is scheduled
to be in Orlando, December 12-15.
So again, just keep those dates in mind.
In the past, you may have heard from our keynote speaker.
Pete Sheen has provided interesting keynote remarks
at two previous Sustainment Series sessions and we invited him back today
to provide current observation, as you will see given how world events are and how interrelated,
not only is readiness to what's going on in economics but there are many opportunities
to see how our global strategy ties to economics.
So, Pete is our global strategy and economics advisor to the joint staff.
Strategy Plans and Policy Directorate, Director's Advisory Group.
He provides the joint staff with analysis of the nexus of economy, energy,
finance for the US National Strategy.
He also provides support to joint staff decisions through applying behavioral,
econometric, and psychometric analytical techniques --
I think that's the first time I've said that word --
and insights in support of national security strategies, policies, and decisions.
So, you can see it's data heavy.
And given our journey and data, let's stand by to be informed and intrigued.
Pete, over to you.
>> Thank you very much.
And, I hope, by the way, if anybody wants to talk
about how cool psychometrics are, I'm happy to talk about that.
But that's not the subject of today's discussion.
So, the previous two times we've done this virtually
from the undisclosed location, I've talked about theme.
As we entered the COVID period and, in particular with y'all, I spent some time talking
about the digital attack surface of the US economy growing.
That hasn't stopped.
As a matter of fact that's accelerated.
But because of current situation, I thought we might step back and I'll give you a sort
of an overview of the current global situation.
And then, after that, what we're going to do is we're going to provide a little insight
into what's going on in Europe right now
from a long term economic perspective with a focus on decarbonization.
So, with that in mind, the idea here is to step back --
as one of the previous chairman identified this -- is to step back and depict those key features
of the strategic environment that are economic in nature that impact US national security.
And if you step back and you do that, there's sort of four themes.
And I'm going to spend just a little bit of time on each one of them.
The first theme where I'm going to spend the most time is multipolar competition.
And, in particular, for this group, I would like for you to think about what are those resources
that you've identified that are going to be necessary for a decarbonized defense enterprise?
Because that's where we seem to be heading, towards decarbonization being applied not just
to private industry but also to US government, including the military.
And as we move towards decarbonization, how do we -- so there's the slide right there.
Thank you for putting that up.
How do we identify those resources that we're going to need as a military to participate
for direction in that decarbonization effort?
And here's where it gets important.
We're not going to be the only ones looking for those resources.
There's going to be a competition for those resources.
And the way this works is just recently, I think it was last year or maybe the year before,
the European commission published a study.
And what they did is they looked at, okay, they identified, I believe, there's 37 resources
that the European defense sector needed, right?
The European defense sector needed these.
I believe it was 37 key minerals.
And then, they looked at where those minerals were drawn from
or where the resources were drawn from.
This makes it, actually they do have an important point here
that many other sources make as well.
Sometimes it doesn't matter where the actual resource came from,
sometimes because the resource has to be processed.
So, what happens is where did the European defense sector get the result of the processing
or the refinement of that resource?
And I'm sure everyone here can guess what the number one country was that was the source
for key resources, key minerals for the European defense sector.
It was the People's Republic of China.
Just recently a leading us bank identified those eight critical minerals --
be careful with that term because that has legal consequences.
I'm not using it in the US government legal sense, I'm using it in the sense
of what the bank was calling, critical minerals for the decarbonization economy
of which rare earths was grouped as just one set.
Of those eight, China was the key source for the US economy as a whole.
China was the number one source.
So, the key point here, what I want you to sort of take away from this decarbonizing resources
within multipolar competition is that there is a story going on.
A story that started in the 1970s when Deng Xiaoping said he wanted China
to be the Saudi Arabia of rare earths.
We're kind of entering this story late.
We don't know -- to switch analogies -- if you ever showed up at a baseball game late,
and you didn't realize you showed up late, and there were three, you know,
four innings had passed and your team was already behind,
we're in at least the fourth inning.
Our team's already behind in the competition for decarbonizing resources.
So, if people can hear, can you please in the chat say you can hear?
Because I just saw a chat saying that someone can't hear.
So, the next thing, there's a lot of folks talking about supply chain.
So, I don't really need -- okay, that's good.
Most folks can hear.
Thank you very much.
So, most folks have already heard about us talking about supply chains,
but I want you to sort of to park on at least one concept before we can move
on in this competition here, is how do we define resilience in a contested environment?
Now, y'all are going to have a panel about this later and that's great
for your for you to discuss this issue.
What I want you to think about based on my reading from the private sector,
is how they're operationalizing their notion of resilient supply chains.
And the answer for many companies is about infusing their supply chains with sensors
and then having those sensors report in real time, the status.
So, in other words, they're digitalizing their supply chains.
Now, in one sense, that's really great, right, from a resilient perspective?
Because now they can have visibility as to what's going on.
Speaking of visibility, if you can't see the slide, all it is, is one slide with a lot
of bullet points and I'm talking to it.
So, you don't have to -- I'm talking all the content
that is relevant to our discussion today.
So, don't feel bad if you can't see the slide, speaking of visibility.
But for visibility and supply chains, what just happened there?
What just happened there when we digitize their supply chains?
What we did is we took the digital attack surface for supply chains,
which was this wide before and made it this wide.
Now, if that's what needs to happen in order to make for resilient supply chains,
then that's what needs to happen.
But there are also is significant security and defense-related implications
for us taking the digital attack surface of our supply chains from this to this.
And because we don't have much time, I'm going to skip past ideas.
I'm going to leave a little time at the end for questions.
So, if you have any questions if that would be great.
Compose if you're interested about the idea of facet, for example.
The next main theme, for those of you who can't see the slide and I apologize,
is called COVID-19 winners and losers.
You may recall during one of these sessions before,
one of the points underneath this main theme was that the US was losing over 3,000 people a day
to COVID-19 and the Chinese, it was maybe one or two.
And so, they were presenting themselves as winners.
But I want to update you on that.
What's happened since then is that the Chinese vaccines have been demonstrated
to be much less effective than the Western vaccines.
And the COVID-zero policy, which is the banner for the Chinese policy of allowing no spread
and using authoritarian means to accomplish
that goal is disrupting many supply chains and people's lives.
A lot of people's lives too.
So, what we've got now is a situation we're in, hold the phone.
China, not necessarily the winner in this struggle against the virus because they have
over a billion people with a high vaccination rate, but it's a poor vaccine.
And now, Omicron is present, which is much more virulent.
Put these together and there's a recipe for supply chain disruption as the authorities
in the People's Republic of China implement their COVID-zero policy and shut down one
of the top five largest ports in the entire world for one case of COVID, for example.
This is important because it's one of those things where, you know,
don't call the game before it's done, right, don't call the game before it's done.
To go back to my baseball analogy, we may be in the fourth inning and behind
but there's still five more innings here.
So, as this virus continues to evolve and as our economic and our political responses,
and mitigation measures, and even adjustment to it, right, as the virus becomes endemic,
that's when we get to the 9th inning and it's not clear yet.
But what is quite important for us to remember is that the Chinese were shouting
from the rooftops of their success in COVID-19 and that success doesn't look so durable now.
That's an important lesson.
The next point, and then we're getting pretty close here
to wrapping this up, has to do with debt legacy.
And to cut to the chase on debt legacy is that, you know, years ago I worked
for Jay [inaudible], one of the budget guys and go figure, a couple of degrees in economics.
And one of the things we talked about were the trade offs, right,
the trade offs in where the US government allocates its spending.
And this isn't just the US government.
This is also, basically, all the governments that that incurred massive amounts
of new debt in response to COVID-19 crisis.
That's going to need to be repaid.
And so, we should be unsurprised to see, not just as we cross the Potomac
but also the equivalents at the Ministry of Defense to Parliament in London, and in France,
and in all the rest in Japan, and South Korea.
All these countries that incurred larger amounts of debt,
they're going to be balancing paying off that debt, other policies, right,
other things they want to do, and defense.
Defense spending will be at play.
We should remember that as a legacy from the COVID-19 crisis.
The debt legacy, increased debt.
And finally, uneven digitization, which was the main focus of the previous two times I did this
from the undisclosed basement location.
So, I'm not going to spend too much time on that with the exception
of we've already talked about, supply chains.
Well, that actually fits towards whole economies as well.
One of the things that's happened during the COVID-19 crisis is we have massively accelerated
trends to pool what was previously not digital, or digitally associated in our economy,
and put it into the digital economy.
Just witness what's happening right now.
Previously, I provided keynote comments to the maintenance symposia in person, right?
Now, I'm coming to you from the undisclosed basement location.
So, before it was in person, now it's digital.
But I did want to make -- because we only have a few minutes left of my time before,
if you have any questions, then plus that.
I did want to make at least two points about what's going on in Russia and Ukraine right now.
From a long-term economic perspective, again, this is a long-term economic perspective.
And I want to remind everybody, if you can't see, the very small print on the on the bottom
of the slide is that all views expressed in this brief are the presenter's own
and in no way represent the views positions of the joint staff,
the Department of Defense for the US government.
So, this is in my capacity as an advisor, everything that I say here.
If you were in charge of a country that, according to you -- so Putin said this --
that over 40% of his government revenues come from hydrocarbons, right?
If you ran a country here over 40% of your government revenue came from hydrocarbons,
and you read the writing on the wall on the trend towards decarbonization,
and the move away from hydrocarbons, step back and think about how
that would affect your conceptualization of a timeline of action, right?
When are you going to have the resources to be able to act
on the international stage in a determinative manner?
When are you going to be able to do that?
And is that on a trajectory up, stable, or down?
And the answer is, well, there will continue to be demand for hydrocarbons.
As, you know, we'll still have feedstock for chemicals and feedstock for plastics.
As hydrocarbons become less and less important for fuel, the market that generates all
that revenue for over 40% of the Kremlin's budget is getting whittled away.
And by the way, while they are a kind of low cost producer,
they're not the low cost producer, which means up against Saudi Arabia or the Permian Basin,
they're very often going to lose business while those other places might continue to thrive
because of their low cost production schedules.
What does that mean for us from a security environment perspective?
It means that, while the popular press talks a lot about V. Putin and his very small group
of other men that he interacts with, it's like four other guys
because he's very afraid of COVID.
And so, he limits people that he talks to and things like that, and the closed loopness
of his discussion points, and his advisors through that.
There might be some real veracity to that.
But what I'm also telling you is a cold-hearted economic look at the viability
of the Russian business model indicates they're on a timeline towards degradation, and less,
and less, and less economic strength upon
which they can build any kind of power in a multipolar world.
And with that, it's subject to your questions.
>> Hey, thanks for that, Pete.
This is Dr. Ramdass.
I'll give the audience a couple of minutes
to formulate a few questions for our keynote speaker.
But just a thought.
So, I like your map, I like the challenges.
What would you assess -- and this is your role as an advisor --
how would you assess the inner agency or more of a whole of society vice whole
of government approach to those challenges?
And you mentioned, also, the role of technology.
And I wonder your thoughts on our use thus far of AI and machine learning to get
after understand some of those and see how they're interrelated and, you know,
to formulate some strategies to go after them.
Over.
>> Those are great questions, thanks.
So, the first one about the whole of society.
If you have a chance, there's an Oxford University report
on the Internet Research Agency which is a unit of the Russian Government.
It was presented to Congress and it talked
about how the Russian government influenced our last election cycle.
It might be something to look at in a sense
of how technology interacts with the whole society approach.
Even as we speak right now, right now, there are fake Facebook --
this according to the open source -- fake Facebook accounts being opened
and then disseminating messages about trying to stop US commerce within US borders,
just like commerce has been stopped at the US/Canadian borders
on the Canadian side, even as we speak.
So, what we're looking at is technology being used to facilitate the voices of disruption.
So, the question here becomes, what are those, how can we use those same technical means
to be able to switch it around to be able to pull us together?
That's a really interesting question.
And the point, if you have a chance, even before many of these things were written,
one of the previous Chairmen of the Joint Staff used to recommend a book called the "End
of Power" by Moises Naim and AIM.
And in this book, his thesis was technology has brought us to a point where the power
to disrupt has been magnified and the power to maintain has been decremented.
And I think that's a powerful point for your first question
about what's inhibiting whole of society approaches?
And I would posit to you actually much of technology inhibits time,
inhibits whole society approaches.
Just really quickly about artificial intelligence and machine learning
that I think that's very important for us to do.
And this is from somebody who -- one of the ways I made my way through one
of my graduate degrees was -- I was one of those people that would log into the mainframe
and then run analysis for professors.
So, my old school analysis not AI
because we didn't have the horsepower to do that at that time.
But I would ask you to seriously think about the data set upon which your machine learned.
Because machine learning is about pattern recognition based
on the data that it can eat, right?
And so, one of the things that I have written about previously in my products for the chairman
and for various military leaders is that we need to be extremely careful in generalizing
from conditions that machines learn from to conflict situations.
And the reason why is because, by definition, conflict is different.
And the example I would like to use and then I'll wrap this up.
But the example I used to like to use is actually interpersonal.
So, I have children.
Maybe you have children as well.
What you'll know from that experience is that there's this situation
where your children are up until they're -- I had boys.
So, up until they're about 13 or 14, you kind of learn how
to interact with them and what works, right?
And then, something happens when they're teenagers.
And those things don't work anymore, right?
Well, I would pose to you just like your relationship with your children
and that social experience and interaction, the interaction of the social,
of the social political economic actors upon
which those machine learning algorithms were generated were about until the kids were 13.
And when conflicts started, they turned into teenagers.
So, be careful applying what worked when they were eight, when they're 16.
Because if you're like me and you fell back on some old habits and if your are like mine,
they probably readily told you that that was inappropriate to help solve the situation.
>> Thank you, Pete.
I don't know if you can see the chat, maybe you can pull one more question
from there and then we can [inaudible].
>> So, one of the really interesting things about the,
from Gregory Kilchenstein [assumed spelling], that's a really interesting question
about economic resources from Ukraine.
It's very difficult to make an economic argument for taking Ukraine because there are competitors
in grain markets there, there's been talk
of them having some natural gas, but it's been difficult to find.
From a resource plan, I would posit that there isn't an argument to take Ukraine.
And I would, you know, what was it, thirty-some pages, the thing that Putin wrote
about how historically Kiev is the mother city for the Rus', right?
I think that's actually the more appropriate framework, but I would ask you to think,
not about resources that they get from Ukraine, but about the price of oil,
specifically, and natural gas too.
But let's focus on oil.
Just recently, Bloomberg published an estimate that said that if Vladimir Putin continues --
and I apologize, I forget how long this would take.
If Vladimir Putin continues to push the price of oil north
of $90 a barrel, he makes an extra $63 billion.
So, what happens here is instead of thinking about this as a resource play, right,
instead think about it as a manipulation play.
And actually, the Iranians were famous for doing this,
famous for doing this with the Strait of Hormuz.
This was before when they used to sell a lot more oil before the sanctions.
What they would do is they'd run some fast boats through the Strait of Hormuz,
price of oil would go up because here's the key phrase, risk premia.
The risk premia would go up and then they'd cash in.
And they were famous for doing this and I would posit to you that possibly Moscow was looking
at [inaudible] track record and thinking
that we could possibly make some serious cash off of this.
Now, I'm not saying that was the sole motivator or the chief motivator, but $63 billion dollars
in reasons, especially when the market pushes down the ruble and your cost basis is
in the ruble, which means you win both ways.
Your costs go down because it's their denominated in rubles, and your revenue goes
up because it's denominated in dollars, and you're making more off every barrel.
That's a smile.
>> Folks, Mr. Pete Steen.
Always riveting and you surely get, you know, thinking caps on,
and stimulator, or intellectual juices.
So, thank you, thank you.
And you have a few questions in there, Pete.
I don't know if you're going to stay with us or if there's a chance you could respond to those.
If not, we'll definitely try to follow up with you with those.
So again, I really appreciate your time today.
Let's give Mr. Pete Steen a virtual round of applause.
>> Well, thanks a lot.
Have a great rest of the day.
>> Awesome, thank you.
So now, we'll transition to our first panel of the day
and that is moving technology into sustainment.
I had a chance earlier, before I joined here, to listen to the hearing, the confirmation hearing
for ASDS nominee, Mr. Chris Lumen [assumed spelling].
And the members post questions that really aligned to both of our panels today.
The first actually dealt with contested logistics, and the tyranny of distance,
and how Mr. Lumen would, what are some of those things he would do in the position as the ASDS.
The second, also, was how will he look at the material readiness and reduce the cost?
And as you will hear from our esteemed panel today, whom I will introduce shortly,
that's some of the things they have been charged with going forward.
So quickly, history here.
We published, last May, the DoD 5000.92, which established policy to develop, and implement,
and expand the application of innovative practices, processes,
and technology for sustaining material readiness across the lifecycle of DoD systems and really,
to improve our industrial base operations.
The key here, though, I want to point out to this audience before we get into the discussion
with our panelists is the fact that we define sustainment technology as the application
of improved processes and technology, right?
So, those tangible things but also what can we do with respect to process improvement
to really take on those challenges?
And over the last few weeks we've had the Joint Technology Exchange Group really working to look
at those common sustainment capability gaps and try to line solutions,
sustainment technology solutions that in their, you know, high level test readiness levels
that can be really fielded quickly to our services.
And quite frankly, that is easier said than done.
There are a number of challenges that you will hear from but there are also a number
of opportunities that our panelists will speak to.
So again, first I want to say I really appreciate our panel this time.
We have Mr. Tim Goddette, the Deputy Assistant Secretary of the Army for Sustainment.
We have Ms. Angela Tymofichuk, the Deputy Assistant Secretary of Air Force
for Acquisition and Product Support.
And we have Mr. Rob Gold, the Director of Technology and Manufacturing
for the Industrial Base in the Office of the Research and Engineering USD R&E.
And so, thank you, panelists.
The first panelist we'll hear from is Mr. Tim Goddette.
And to really share with you what the Army is doing in terms of opportunity challenges
and opportunities that relates to implementing 5000.92.
And then, we'll go to Ms. T, then followed up by Rob Gold.
So, with that, over to you Tim.
Tim, if you're speaking, you might be on mute.
>> Yep, nope, I'm there.
Thanks, thanks Dr. Ramdass.
I really appreciate it.
I'd like to say good morning to all and thanks to Dr. Ramdass for the opportunity to engage
on this panel today Angie and Rob to discuss moving technology and sustainment.
I'm going to probably stay on the theme that Vic mentioned that it's not just technology alone.
He mentioned process as well.
And so, as a scene setter, I'd like to take a take you a little bit off course
and then bring us back.
I'm sure many of you can remember the show "Mythbusters."
Well, today I'm going to challenge a long-stated myth that 70%
of the weapons systems lifecycle costs are in sustainment or logistics.
And I guess a lot of you may be thinking, well,
why would the Army's [inaudible] for sustainment even say that?
And what I hope to do is make a point.
How we spend our money should probably provide us a little bit of insight.
And so, what I hope at the end is we look at is 70% really being spent in that area?
What I did was I took a look at the FY 21 Army budget and I did a little bit of rounding
as well, but not a lot to just to kind of make the point.
In 2021, the Army's budget was about $170 billion dollars.
And when you take out the portion related to weapons systems,
in the Army that would be our equipping peg, our sustaining peg and our training peg.
It came out to about 53 billion.
And so, when I look at that $53 billion and I look at how much is in equipping, which was 38.
That only left 15 for readiness.
Those things with parts and, you know, fuel maintenance, et cetera.
When you look at that, the readiness for the sustainment part was only 30%
and the equipping which included RDT&E was 70%.
So, it was actually flipped.
And so, when you dig a little bit deeper, what that really meant was what's missing?
And what's missing is the people.
In the Army we're a little different than the other services.
Military paying allowances make up about 40% of our budget.
And so, the Army spends more on people than we do
on equipping, modernizing, and/or sustainment.
We used to say, you know, that the other services man their equipment
and the Army equips their men, right?
So, I guess after you look at that, the myth that 70% goes
to logistics is partly busted unless you're clear that the 70%,
when you look at the life cycle support costs of any weapons systems,
the O&S costs actually include the people, the manpower.
And in our service, the Army, that is significant.
So, why did I make that point?
I think when you look at that, that would probably get many people to kind
of shift the narrative or to drive behavior, maybe, when you look at technology or you look
at processes to focus more on time and or the number of soldiers it takes
to either operate the equipment, to conduct preventive maintenance checks and services,
for mechanics to do the troubleshooting, and the actual wrench turning,
or for the supply side in units to order parts.
So, if we take and start at the unit and work our way backwards, whether it's better design
of the equipment for ease of operations, or maintenance, or whether it's other technologies
that help reduce the burden on soldiers, or the time it takes to maintain a piece of equipment.
It really should include reengineering the legacy process
if we're going to make a difference.
And so, bottom line moving technology into sustainment alone,
just the technology is not enough.
And I'd like to give an example, if I can and then I'll turn it over to Angie.
So, in the Army, when we talk about the maintenance process that would go
with technology, we're still using a process that's largely paper based.
Our operators, when they do their preventative maintenance checks
and services, use paper forms, right?
They use paper technical manuals, in a lot of cases, to capture the actions
on their particular weapons systems.
And when they identify problems to send to the mechanics, they're writing it again
on paper that's handed over to the mechanic.
Our operators don't have electronic devices like templates or smartphones --
I'm sorry, tablets or smartphones -- it's still paper.
Our mechanics, over the years, are given tools.
And in this case, most of our mechanics have laptops but they don't interface very well.
They're not intuitive, they're not linked to the vehicle easily,
and they definitely don't take the information and then provide it
through into the supply process that we have for ordering parts.
And when it's turned over to our parts clerks to order the parts, when you go from paper
into a computer and then from computer back to paper, there's a lot of opportunities
for mistakes when you're retyping.
There's also the opportunity to delink a part from the particular exact weapons system
or the conditions in which something might have failed, like, the miles or the hours.
And therefore, jumping from the traditional maintenance into condition-based maintenance
and using data properly is further complicated.
So, I know we have the technology.
The technology is out there but we have to spend more time, I believe, linking that technology
in the process or reinventing the process, and then focusing on the man machine interface.
Technology alone is not going to move us where we need to be.
We have to link that technology very, very well with the people that are using it
and the processes that we're creating as we move from operators, to mechanics, to supply,
and then back as we try to ensure that the equipment that we're fielding is ready to go
when we need it and to keep it in the fight.
So, I think I'll end right there.
That's really that the point that I wanted to make.
One, that the Army is very focused on the operator,
on the manpower, if you will, the soldier.
And therefore, we need to do a good job linking it to saving time and saving the number
of soldiers we have to do the mission because we're not getting more money.
That was brought up, I think, by Pete.
